column3: First half has 7 Caturmātras and a long letter at the end; second has 5 Caturmātras followed by 1 short letter, 1 Caturmātra and 1 long letter. Thus the two halves have 30 and 27 Mātrās respectively. In each half the Caturmātras in odd places must not be a Jagaṇa (ISI). The 6th Caturmātra in the first half must be either Jagaṇa (ISI) or Sarvalaghu (IIII). In the latter case a new word must begin with the 2nd Laghu. But if the 7th Gaṇa of the 1st half or the 5th Gaṇa of the 2nd are of the Sarvalaghu type, a new word must begin with the 1st Laghu.
When a Yati is clearly felt at the end of the 3rd Caturmātra, the Āryā is called Pathyā.

When a Yati is not clearly felt at the end of the 3rd Caturmātra, i e., when only 1 letter of a word commenced in the 3rd Caturmātra belongs to either the 3rd or the 4th Caturmātra, the Āryā is called Vipulā.

When the 2nd and the 4th Caturmātras of an Āryā are Jagaṇas (1S1), both preceded and followed by a long letter, it is called Capalā. When this happens only in the first half, it is Mukhacapalā; when only in the second, it is Jaghanacapala.
When the 2nd half of an Āryā wholly resembles the 1st, it is called Gīti.
When the 1st half of an Āryā wholly resembles the 2nd, it is called Upagīti.
When the two halves of an Āryā exchange their places, it is called Udgīti.

When each half of an Āryā contains 8 Caturmātras, it is called Āryāgīti or Skandhaka. According to some writers like Sulhaṇa, it is an Āryā extended by 2 Mātrās in each half; so that its two halves have respectively 32 and 29 Mātrās in them.
